ln -sf TARGET LINKNAME -- what do -s and -f do?
column2:
-s = symbolic link (a path pointer; crosses filesystems, can point at dirs).
-f = force: remove an existing LINKNAME first, so re-runs stay idempotent.

column1: Symlinked script runs locally, but a fresh git clone isn't executable. Fix?
column2:
Commit the +x bit at the source, not through the link:
git update-index --chmod=+x path/to/script   (mode 100644 -> 100755)
chmod through a symlink only changes your local target's mode; the repo still ships 644.

column1: find: list only BROKEN (dangling) symlinks?
column2:
find . -xtype l
-type l = the link itself (working OR broken); -xtype checks the TARGET, so a healthy
link resolves to f/d and is never 'l' -- only a broken one reports as 'l'.

column1: In zsh/bash, test whether fd 1 (stdout) is a terminal?
column2:
[[ -t 1 ]]
-t N tests fd N; false for pipes, redirects, and non-interactive / no-pty shells.
(-t 0 = stdin, -t 2 = stderr)

column1: TTY vs PTY?
column2:
tty = kernel device for a terminal endpoint (I/O, line editing, signals, controlling term).
pty = software tty when there's no hardware terminal. Two ends: MASTER (emulator/tmux/ssh
holds it) and SLAVE (/dev/pts/N, what your shell sees as its tty).

column1: wsl.exe: run a command INSIDE the distro after its own flags?
column2:
wsl.exe -d Debian --cd ~ -- env NO_TMUX=1 zsh -li
-- ends wsl.exe's own options; everything after runs inside the distro.

column1: Set an env var for just one command's process, then exec it?
column2:
env VAR=val cmd
e.g. env NO_TMUX=1 zsh -li  -- sets NO_TMUX, then execs an interactive-login zsh with it.

column1: Which two signals cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored?
column2:
SIGKILL (9) and SIGSTOP (19). The kernel handles them directly -- that's why kill -9
always works and why you can't trap it to run cleanup.

column1: kill's default signal, and why prefer it over -9?
column2:
SIGTERM (15) is the default. It lets the program run its cleanup (EXIT/TERM trap).
SIGKILL (9) skips all cleanup -- last resort only, after SIGTERM fails.

column1: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, Ctrl-backslash send which signals?
column2:
Ctrl-C = SIGINT, Ctrl-Z = SIGTSTP, Ctrl-backslash = SIGQUIT.
Sent to the terminal's foreground process group.

column1: `for SIG in "$(kill -l)"` runs once with everything joined. Why, and the fix?
column2:
Double quotes make the whole output ONE word (no splitting). Drop them:
for SIG in $(kill -l); do echo "$SIG"; done
The rare case where you WANT word-splitting. (Or: kill -l | tr ' ' '\n')

column1: Check whether fg/bg is a builtin or a file on disk?
column2:
type fg    -> "fg is a shell builtin"
type -a NAME shows ALL matches (aliases + files). Builtins have no $PATH entry, so
which / command -v can mislead. fg/bg MUST be builtins -- they touch the shell's job table.

column1: Test GitHub SSH auth without requesting a shell?
column2:
ssh -T git@github.com
-T = don't allocate a PTY (GitHub gives no shell). Success is the greeting:
"Hi <user>! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access."

column1: ssh -T vs ssh -t?
column2:
-T = do NOT allocate a PTY (for services with no interactive shell, like GitHub).
-t = force-allocate a PTY.

column1: git push over SSH -> "Permission denied (publickey)". First things to check?
column2:
ssh -vT git@github.com   (shows which keys are offered and why refused)
1. perms: chmod 700 ~/.ssh; 600 private key; 644 .pub
2. .pub registered on GitHub settings
3. remote is HTTPS not SSH -> git remote set-url origin git@github.com:USER/REPO.git

column1: git push asks for a password and fails. Why, and the fix?
column2:
GitHub removed HTTPS password auth (2021); the remote is HTTPS. Switch to SSH:
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:USER/REPO.git

column1: tmux: y is only copy-selection-and-cancel -- why does it still copy to the system clipboard?
column2:
OSC 52 via set-clipboard (default 'external'). On copy, tmux emits an OSC 52 escape
sequence to the outer terminal, which sets the system clipboard. Fires on EVERY copy,
independent of copy-command. WezTerm supports OSC 52 -> it lands on the Windows clipboard.

column1: Which tmux copy commands use copy-command (e.g. clip.exe)?
column2:
Only copy-pipe* bindings (copy-pipe-and-cancel with no arg pipes to copy-command).
copy-selection* does NOT use it -- but still reaches the clipboard via OSC 52.

column1: tmux set-clipboard: external vs on?
column2:
external (default): tmux sets the OUTER terminal's clipboard on copy; ignores OSC 52
from apps inside tmux.
on: same, PLUS accepts OSC 52 from inside apps (needed for nested tmux).
off: no OSC 52.
Check: tmux show -gv set-clipboard

column1: Symptom: "open terminal failed: not a terminal" when auto-starting tmux from .zshrc. Cause?
column2:
The exec tmux block ran with no real TTY -- it sat BELOW p10k's instant-prompt block,
which grabbed the TTY first. Fix: move it ABOVE the instant-prompt block and guard with
[[ -t 1 ]].

column1: The guards on the .zshrc tmux auto-start line, and why each?
column2:
[[ -z "$TMUX" ]]        not already in tmux (inner shell re-sources .zshrc)
[[ -z "${NO_TMUX:-}" ]] opt-out escape hatch
[[ -o interactive ]]    interactive shells only
[[ -t 1 ]]              fd 1 is a real tty (cures "not a terminal")
command -v tmux         don't error if tmux is missing

column1: tmux: mode-keys vi is set, but v makes a block selection instead of a normal one. Why?
column2:
mode-keys vi only sets NAVIGATION. On recent tmux, v defaults to rectangle-toggle.
For nvim-like visual mode you must bind it:
bind-key -T copy-mode-vi 'v' send -X begin-selection
(default copy keys are Space = begin-selection, Enter = copy-and-cancel)

column1: WezTerm: two entries bound to the same key+mods -- what happens?
column2:
The LAST entry in the keys table wins; the earlier one silently does nothing.
Audit with: wezterm show-keys. Fix by moving one action to a free key.

column1: Is a symlinked ~/.p10k.zsh safe? When could it break?
column2:
Safe day-to-day: p10k is a THEME, sourced (read) each shell start -- reading never breaks
a symlink. Only `p10k configure` (a manual WRITE) rewrites ~/.p10k.zsh and can replace the
link with a regular file -- re-run ln -sf afterward.

column1: What does `set -euo pipefail` do (each flag)?
column2:
-e  exit on any command's non-zero exit
-u  unset variable is an error
-o pipefail  a pipe fails if ANY stage fails (no single-letter form)

column1: ${VAR:-default} vs ${VAR-default} -- the colon?
column2:
:-  use default if VAR is unset OR empty
-   use default only if VAR is truly unset (empty stays empty)
The colon means "treat empty as unset too". Same rule for :+ / + and :? / ?.

column1: Under set -u, test "is VAR set?" without crashing on unset?
column2:
${VAR+x} -> "x" if set (even if empty), "" if unset. Never touches VAR's value.
[[ -n "${VAR+x}" ]]   # set (maybe empty)
[[ -n "${VAR:+x}" ]]  # set AND non-empty

column1: ${VAR:?message} does what?
column2:
Use VAR if set+non-empty; otherwise print "VAR: message" to stderr and EXIT.
Guard for required variables.

column1: [[ ]] string/file tests: empty, non-empty, is-file, is-dir, non-empty-file?
column2:
[[ -z "$V" ]]  empty
[[ -n "$V" ]]  non-empty
[ -f PATH ]    regular file exists
[ -d PATH ]    directory exists
[ -s PATH ]    exists AND non-empty
[ ! -f PATH ]  does NOT exist

column1: Numeric comparison operators in [[ ]]?
column2:
-eq -ne -lt -gt -le -ge   (equal, not-equal, <, >, <=, >=)
e.g. [[ $N -gt 5 ]]. Note: == / < are for strings, these for numbers.

column1: Why is `A && B || C` NOT a safe if/else?
column2:
C also runs if B fails (not just when A fails). Safe only when B can't fail
(like echo). Otherwise use a real if.

column1: $(( )) is integer-only. Do float division and format to 2 decimals?
column2:
awk 'BEGIN { printf "%.2f\n", 10 / 3 }'   # 3.33
or: echo "scale=2; 10 / 3" | bc          # 3.33

column1: Compare two floats in a bash condition?
column2:
bash [[ ]] can't. bc returns 1/0:
if (( $(echo "3.5 > 2.1" | bc -l) )); then echo bigger; fi

column1: Send both stdout and stderr of a command to a file?
column2:
command &> file            # overwrite
command &>> file           # append
command > file 2>&1        # equivalent; ORDER matters (stdout->file first)

column1: The three standard file descriptors?
column2:
fd 0 = stdin (inbox), fd 1 = stdout (normal out), fd 2 = stderr (errors, kept
separate so you can redirect it independently).

column1: `echo "oops" >&2` -- what does >&2 mean?
column2:
Send this output to fd 2 (stderr). The & means "the file descriptor numbered 2",
not a file named 2. Without &, >2 would create a file called 2.

column1: Here-doc: expand variables vs print literally?
column2:
cat << EOF      -> $HOME expands
cat << 'EOF'    -> quoted delimiter: $HOME printed literally
Here-string (single line to stdin): cmd <<< "text"

column1: Write a root-owned file from a heredoc (plain > is denied). How?
column2:
sudo tee /etc/some.conf << EOF ... EOF
tee runs AS root; a plain `sudo cmd > file` redirect runs in YOUR shell and is denied.
Add tee -a to append.

column1: Diff the OUTPUT of two commands (no temp files)?
column2:
diff <(cmd1) <(cmd2)
<(cmd) turns a command's output into a temporary filename (/dev/fd/63) that
file-expecting commands can read.

column1: Array basics: all elements, count, last element?
column2:
"${arr[@]}"   all elements (each a separate word)
"${#arr[@]}"  count
"${arr[-1]}"  last
Always quote "${arr[@]}" -- only that form preserves elements with spaces.

column1: "${arr[@]}" vs "${arr[*]}" (quoted)?
column2:
[@] -> each element a SEPARATE word (what you want)
[*] -> all joined into ONE word by IFS
Unquoted, both just split on whitespace. Same rule as "$@" vs "$*".

column1: "$@" vs "$*", and which to forward args unchanged?
Consume positional args one at a time in a while loop?
column2:
while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do
  case "$1" in
    --swap) ... ;;
    *) echo "unknown: $1"; exit 1 ;;
  esac
  shift    # $2->$1, decrements $#
done

column1: Why `local` inside a bash function?
column2:
Scopes the variable to the function. Without it, vars leak to global scope and
can clobber outer variables. local username="$1"

column1: Bash special variables: $# $? $$ $! $0 ?
column2:
$#  arg count
$?  exit code of last command
$$  PID of current script
$!  PID of last background command
$0  script name

column1: Regex match with capture groups in [[ ]] -- where do groups land?
column2:
[[ "$s" =~ ([a-z]+)-([0-9]+) ]]   # pattern UNquoted
${BASH_REMATCH[0]}  whole match
${BASH_REMATCH[1]}  group 1
ERE only: no \d, no (?:...); use [0-9].

column1: Why does sed need backslashes: \? \+ \( \) but grep -E doesn't?
column2:
sed defaults to BRE where ? + ( ) | are LITERAL and must be escaped to activate.
ERE (grep -E, sed -E, [[ =~ ]]) makes them special by default. Opposite worlds.

column1: Parameter-expansion string ops: length, substring, uppercase, replace-all?
column2:
${#S}         length
${S:0:8}      substring (start, len)
${S^^}        uppercase   (${S,,} lowercase)
${S//o/0}     replace all (${S/o/0} first only)

column1: export a variable so child processes inherit it -- and prove it?
column2:
export NAME              # marks it as env var for children
GREETING="hi"; bash -c 'echo "$GREETING"'   # empty (not inherited)
export GREETING; bash -c 'echo "$GREETING"' # hi

column1: Read a KEY=value file's vars into a subshell to grab one value?
column2:
DISTRO_ID="$(. /etc/os-release && echo "$ID")"   # -> debian / ubuntu
. FILE (== source) runs it in the CURRENT shell, so its vars become available.
Only source files you trust -- it executes them.

column1: Guarantee a temp dir is cleaned up however the script exits?
column2:
tmp="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT
EXIT fires on normal exit, `exit`, set -e failure, and after signals -- the catch-all.

column1: Report which line/command failed, on error?
column2:
trap 'echo "line $LINENO: [$BASH_COMMAND] exited $?" >&2' ERR
$LINENO current line, $BASH_COMMAND the command that ran, $? its exit code.

column1: Read input safely: prompt, hidden (password), raw?
column2:
read -rp "Continue? [y/N] " ans   # -r raw (backslash literal), -p prompt
read -rsp "Pass: " pw             # -s silent (no echo)
Always include -r.

column1: Merge a directory's CONTENTS (incl. dotfiles) into another, no nesting?
column2:
cp -rT src dst      # -T: treat dst as the dir itself, don't nest
cp -r src/. dst/    # the /. = contents incl. hidden files
(cp -r src dst when dst exists -> nests as dst/src)

column1: Skip existing files on copy without erroring (GNU)?
column2:
cp --update=none ...   # modern GNU form
cp -n is DEPRECATED on GNU (Debian warns). Avoid it.

column1: `find ... -exec rm -f {} +` errors "Is a directory" on dirs. Fix?
column2:
Use -r: rm -f does NOT recurse into directories; rm -r does.
find /tmp -iname 'tmp.*' -exec rm -r {} +

column1: find: OR two name patterns and run one -exec on the group?
column2:
find . -type f \( -name '*.pub' -o -name 'known_hosts*' \) -exec chmod 644 {} +
\( \) group (escaped), -o = OR, {} + batches (vs \; = one call per file).

column1: `find -name 'tmp.*'` vs `fd 'tmp.*'` -- same pattern, different meaning?
column2:
find -name: GLOB -- the dot is LITERAL, * = any run of chars.
fd: REGEX -- . = any char, * = zero+ of the preceding atom.
fd is also recursive/regex by default and skips hidden+gitignored.

column1: Pipe a remote script to bash and pass it args?
column2:
curl -fsSL https://.../setup.sh | bash -s -- --swap 1G
curl: -f fail on HTTP error, -s silent, -S show real errors, -L follow redirects.
bash -s reads stdin; -- ends bash's opts, rest goes to the SCRIPT.

column1: Idempotent guard vs failure-swallow: the two || idioms?
column2:
GUARD:   [ -f .env ] || cp .env.example .env    # do it unless already done
SWALLOW: grep -q X file || true                 # let it fail without killing set -e

column1: Add a host to known_hosts non-interactively (only if missing)?
column2:
ssh-keygen -F github.com >/dev/null 2>&1 || ssh-keyscan github.com >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts
ssh-keygen -F = "already known?" (exit 0 if yes). Avoids the authenticity prompt hanging a script.

column1: Three ways to build the range 1..5 in TS/JS?
column2:
for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) ...
Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => i + 1)
[...Array(5).keys()].map(i => i + 1)
